subject: biology
title: A2.1 Origins of cells
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: A2.1 Origins of cells — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic A2.1.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering A2.1 Origins of cells, guide topic A2.1.
final_note: You worked through A2.1 Origins of cells — 9 guide statements.

concepts.def: The Earth before life existed, more than about 4 billion years ago. Its atmosphere contained no free oxygen and therefore no ozone, and had higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane than today. These greenhouse gases kept temperatures higher than at present, and without ozone, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface. Under these conditions a variety of carbon compounds may have formed spontaneously by chemical processes that do not now occur.

Ozone (O₃) is produced in the upper atmosphere from oxygen (O₂) by the action of ultraviolet light, and it absorbs much of the ultraviolet radiation arriving from the Sun. Because pre-biotic Earth had no free oxygen there was no ozone, so ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface of land and water. This radiation supplied energy for chemical reactions but also broke down complex molecules.

The spontaneous formation of carbon compounds such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotide bases from simple inorganic molecules by chemical processes, without any living organism. On pre-biotic Earth, energy from ultraviolet light, lightning and volcanic heat acting on gases such as methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour could produce these compounds. Because the atmosphere now contains free oxygen, which oxidizes such compounds, and because these gases are far less abundant, the same processes do not now occur naturally.

concepts.term: Cell as the smallest unit of self-sustaining life
concepts.def: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the functions of life – metabolism, growth, response to the environment, homeostasis and reproduction – using its own machinery, given a supply of nutrients and energy. A cell contains the enzymes, genetic material and membranes that sustain it; nothing smaller, such as an organelle, a virus or a molecule, can maintain itself independently.

A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), in some cases with a lipid envelope taken from a host cell membrane. Viruses have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism of their own and can only replicate by using the machinery of a host cell. They are considered non-living for these reasons, even though they carry genes and evolve by natural selection.

The principle that a new cell is produced only by division of a pre-existing cell. No process is known today that produces a cell directly from non-living matter, and cells are highly complex, which is why explaining the spontaneous origin of the first cells is a challenge.

concepts.term: Requirements for the evolution of the first cells
concepts.def: Four processes that must have arisen for the first cells to evolve: catalysis (speeding up chemical reactions, before enzymes made by cells existed), self-replication of molecules (copying of information-carrying molecules such as RNA), self-assembly (spontaneous organization of molecules into structures such as bilayers) and the emergence of compartmentalization (enclosure of molecules by a membrane so that the chemistry inside could differ from that outside).

A hypothesized self-organized, membrane-bound compartment containing self-replicating molecules, regarded as a precursor of the first true cells. Protocells had no hard parts and did not fossilize, so their existence is inferred from experiments and from the properties of living cells rather than observed directly.

The requirement that a scientific hypothesis or theory must make predictions that could in principle be shown to be wrong by observation or experiment. Hypotheses about the origin of cells are difficult to test because the exact conditions on pre-biotic Earth cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize, so scientists test them indirectly through laboratory simulations, model systems and evidence from the genomes of living organisms.

An experiment carried out in 1953 in which Stanley Miller and Harold Urey circulated a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, representing the early atmosphere, past electrical sparks that simulated lightning. Water was boiled to supply vapour and a condenser returned the products to a flask representing the ocean. After a week the water contained amino acids and other carbon compounds, showing that carbon compounds needed by life can form from inorganic molecules under conditions that may have existed on pre-biotic Earth.

Strengths: it was the first demonstration that carbon compounds used by living organisms, including several amino acids, form spontaneously from inorganic gases given an energy source, and reanalysis of Miller's stored samples with modern methods found more amino acids than were originally reported. Limitations: the early atmosphere is now thought to have contained more carbon dioxide and nitrogen and less methane and ammonia than the mixture used; the experiment produced only small molecules, not polymers, self-replicating molecules or cells; and the products were an undirected mixture that included many compounds, such as amino acids not used in proteins, that living organisms do not use to build their macromolecules. Later experiments using revised gas mixtures also produced amino acids, so the central conclusion stands.

A molecule with a hydrophilic (polar) part and a hydrophobic (non-polar) part is amphipathic. A fatty acid is amphipathic: its carboxyl group is hydrophilic and its hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic. In water, amphipathic molecules arrange themselves so that the hydrophilic parts remain in contact with water and the hydrophobic parts are excluded from it.

A small spherical sac of fluid enclosed by a membrane. Fatty acids in water can coalesce spontaneously into a bilayer, with hydrophobic tails pointing inwards and hydrophilic heads facing the water on both surfaces, and the bilayer closes on itself to form a sphere. This self-assembly needs no enzymes and creates a membrane-bound compartment in which the internal chemistry can become different from that of the surrounding water.

The hypothesis that RNA was the first genetic material and that the earliest cells used RNA both to store hereditary information and to catalyse reactions, before DNA and protein enzymes evolved. It rests on two properties of RNA: it can be replicated by complementary base pairing, and some RNA molecules have catalytic activity.

An RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst. In the ribosome, the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids during translation is catalysed by ribosomal RNA in the large subunit, not by protein. This surviving ribozyme is evidence that RNA could have acted as the enzymes of the earliest cells.

The most recent organism from which every organism alive today is descended. LUCA was not the first living cell: other forms of life are likely to have evolved before or alongside it, but they became extinct through competition from LUCA and its descendants, leaving LUCA's lineage as the only one with living descendants.

The correspondence between the 64 mRNA codons and the amino acids or stop signals they specify, which is the same in all organisms apart from a few minor variations. Because the assignment of codons to amino acids is largely arbitrary rather than chemically necessary, a shared code is best explained by inheritance from a common ancestor. The presence of shared genes across all organisms, such as those for ribosomal RNA, is a second line of evidence for LUCA.

The oldest widely accepted evidence of cells is microfossils and stromatolites (layered structures built up by microbial communities) in rocks about 3.5 billion years old. These are dated by radiometric dating of the surrounding rock, using the known decay rate of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238; radiocarbon dating cannot be used because carbon-14 decays away within about 50 000 years. Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, so cells existed within the first billion years and life has been evolving for most of Earth's history.

A method of estimating the time since two lineages diverged from the number of differences between their DNA or protein sequences, assuming that mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate that can be calibrated using fossils of known age. Applied to genes shared by all organisms, molecular clocks estimate that LUCA lived roughly 4 billion years ago, but such estimates carry wide uncertainty and cannot be checked against a fossil of LUCA itself.

A fissure in the seafloor from which water heated by magma below emerges, carrying dissolved minerals and reduced compounds such as hydrogen and hydrogen sulfide that precipitate to build chimney-like structures. Vents supply chemical energy, temperature and chemical gradients and mineral catalysts in the absence of sunlight, and are the environment in which LUCA is thought to have evolved.

Microscopic tubes and filaments of iron oxide found in rocks that formed from seafloor hydrothermal vent precipitates in the Nuvvuagittuq belt of Quebec, Canada, dated at least 3.77 billion years old, resemble the iron-oxidizing bacteria that live around vents today. They are interpreted as fossils of some of the earliest life, in the kind of environment in which LUCA is thought to have evolved.

A DNA or protein sequence that has stayed very similar across widely separated lineages because natural selection removes changes to it. Genes found in both bacteria and archaea are inferred to have been present in LUCA. Genomic analysis of such conserved genes indicates that LUCA lived without oxygen, at high temperatures, and used hydrogen and carbon dioxide as its sources of energy and carbon, all of which fit the conditions at hydrothermal vents.

mcqs.q: On pre-biotic Earth, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface far more than it does today. What is the reason for this?
options: There was no free oxygen, so no ozone could form to absorb the radiation.
The methane and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere had destroyed the ozone layer.
Free oxygen was used up oxidizing methane before it could form ozone.
The high temperatures broke down ozone as fast as it was produced.
mcqs.specStatementText: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
mcqs.explain: Ozone (O₃) is made from oxygen (O₂) by ultraviolet light in the upper atmosphere. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet radiation was not absorbed and reached the surface.
rationales: Ozone (O₃) is made from oxygen (O₂) by ultraviolet light in the upper atmosphere. Pre-biotic Earth lacked free oxygen and therefore lacked ozone, so ultraviolet radiation was not absorbed and reached the surface.

A student who pictures the ozone layer as an independent shield that gases can damage picks this. There was no ozone layer to destroy: ozone is formed from oxygen, and pre-biotic Earth had no free oxygen.

A student who assumes oxygen has always been in the air looks for a reason it failed to make ozone. In fact there was no free oxygen at all on pre-biotic Earth; it accumulated only after photosynthetic organisms evolved.

A student who uses the heat of early Earth to explain every early condition picks this. The higher temperatures were a consequence of greenhouse gases; the lack of ozone was a consequence of the lack of oxygen, not of temperature.

mcqs.q: A variety of carbon compounds is thought to have formed spontaneously on pre-biotic Earth. Why do the same processes not produce these compounds naturally on Earth today?
options: Carbon compounds can only be produced by the metabolism of living cells.
The atmosphere now contains free oxygen, which oxidizes such compounds as they form.
Oxygen was present then as now, so something else must have stopped the processes.
The same reactions occur today, but living organisms consume the products first.
mcqs.specStatementText: Early Earth's conditions let carbon compounds form without life
mcqs.explain: The pre-biotic atmosphere lacked free oxygen and was rich in methane and carbon dioxide, with ultraviolet light reaching the surface. Today free oxygen oxidizes carbon compounds and the reducing gases are scarce, so these chemical processes no longer occur.
rationales: A student who believes organic compounds need a living source picks this. Carbon compounds form by ordinary chemistry given reactants and energy; the pre-biotic conditions supplied both, which is the point of the statement.

The pre-biotic atmosphere lacked free oxygen and was rich in methane and carbon dioxide, with ultraviolet light reaching the surface. Today free oxygen oxidizes carbon compounds and the reducing gases are scarce, so these chemical processes no longer occur.

A student who assumes oxygen has always been part of the air picks this and looks for some other explanation. In fact the pre-biotic atmosphere had no free oxygen at all; oxygen accumulated only after photosynthetic organisms evolved, and its presence today is precisely why these chemical processes no longer occur.

A student who thinks the pre-biotic processes are still running picks this. The IB guide states that these compounds formed by chemical processes that do not now occur; the oxygen-rich atmosphere prevents them, whether or not organisms are present.

mcqs.q: Which statement gives a reason that viruses are considered to be non-living?
options: They are cells that are too small to hold the organelles needed for metabolism.
They are not whole organisms, and only complete organisms are living.
They carry out no metabolism and can only replicate using a host cell.
They have genes and can evolve, but they do not have a nucleus.
mcqs.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
mcqs.explain: A virus has no enzymes for metabolism and cannot grow, respond or maintain itself. New virus particles are made by the host cell's machinery, so a virus is not self-sustaining, which is why it is considered non-living.
rationales: A student who thinks of a virus as a very small cell picks this. A virus is not a cell of any size: it is genetic material in a protein coat with no cytoplasm, ribosomes or membrane-enclosed interior.

A student who regards only whole organisms as living picks this. Being an organism is not the criterion: a bacterium is a single cell and is alive. Viruses are non-living because they lack metabolism and cannot replicate independently, whatever their size or organization.

A virus has no enzymes for metabolism and cannot grow, respond or maintain itself. New virus particles are made by the host cell's machinery, so a virus is not self-sustaining, which is why it is considered non-living.

A student who counts viruses as living because they have genes and evolve looks for a structural reason and picks the missing nucleus, but bacteria also lack a nucleus and are alive. Viruses are non-living because they have no metabolism and cannot replicate without a host cell.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the smallest unit that can sustain itself as living, given only nutrients and a source of energy?
options: A whole multicellular animal
A virus inside a host cell
A mitochondrion in a cell
A free-living bacterium
mcqs.specStatementText: The cell is the smallest thing that keeps itself alive
mcqs.explain: A bacterial cell carries out metabolism, growth, response, homeostasis and reproduction using its own enzymes, genetic material and membranes. The cell is the smallest unit of self-sustaining life.
rationales: A student who regards only whole organisms as living picks this. Cells are alive in their own right, and unicellular organisms show that a single cell can sustain all the functions of life.

A student who counts viruses as living because they reproduce picks this. A virus does not sustain itself: the host cell's metabolism and ribosomes make the new particles, so the virus is not a self-sustaining unit.

A student who thinks respiring organelles with their own DNA are alive picks this. A mitochondrion depends on the cell for most of its proteins and cannot survive or reproduce outside it, so it is not self-sustaining.
A bacterial cell carries out metabolism, growth, response, homeostasis and reproduction using its own enzymes, genetic material and membranes. The cell is the smallest unit of self-sustaining life.

mcqs.q: Which set of processes is regarded as the necessary requirements for the evolution of the first cells?
options: Catalysis, self-replication of molecules, self-assembly and the emergence of compartmentalization
A single improbable chance event assembling a complete cell with all of its parts at once
Formation of DNA, then transcription and translation, before any membrane had formed
Continuing spontaneous generation of whole cells from non-living matter in pond water
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the first cells are hard to explain
mcqs.explain: These four processes are the requirements named in the IB guide: reactions had to be speeded up, information-carrying molecules had to be copied, structures had to organize themselves, and a membrane-bound compartment had to separate internal chemistry from the outside.
rationales: These four processes are the requirements named in the IB guide: reactions had to be speeded up, information-carrying molecules had to be copied, structures had to organize themselves, and a membrane-bound compartment had to separate internal chemistry from the outside.

A student who reads 'spontaneous' as 'all at once' picks this. No scientist proposes a complete cell assembling by chance; the origin of cells is explained as a sequence of processes that could each occur spontaneously.

A student who assumes DNA had to come first picks this. The first genetic material is presumed to have been RNA, and compartmentalization is one of the requirements, not something that came only after a full DNA-based system.

A student who thinks cells still arise from non-living matter picks this. Cells are currently produced only by division of pre-existing cells; the requirements listed in the guide describe how the first cells could have emerged under conditions that no longer exist.

mcqs.q: A student claims that the hypothesis that the first cells arose spontaneously on pre-biotic Earth is not scientific, because the event cannot be observed. Which response is the best evaluation of this claim?
options: The claim is correct, because an event that cannot be directly observed or repeated lies outside science.
It is testable indirectly, though hard to test because the exact conditions cannot be replicated.
The claim is wrong, because the Miller–Urey experiment has already confirmed how the first cells formed.
The claim is wrong, because the spontaneous formation of cells can still be observed in ponds today.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why the first cells are hard to explain
mcqs.explain: Claims in science must be testable, and this hypothesis makes testable predictions – that carbon compounds, vesicles and catalytic RNA form under plausible conditions. Scientists struggle with it because the exact pre-biotic conditions cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize, but difficulty is not untestability.
rationales: A student who equates 'testable' with 'directly observable' picks this. Scientific claims must be testable, but testing can be indirect, through predictions checked by simulations, model systems and evidence from living organisms.

Claims in science must be testable, and this hypothesis makes testable predictions – that carbon compounds, vesicles and catalytic RNA form under plausible conditions. Scientists struggle with it because the exact pre-biotic conditions cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize, but difficulty is not untestability.

A student who believes Miller and Urey produced life picks this. Their experiment provided evidence only that carbon compounds can form abiotically; it did not test the later steps or confirm the origin of cells.

A student who thinks cells still arise from non-living matter picks this. Cells are currently produced only by division of pre-existing cells; the origin of the first cells cannot be watched happening now.

mcqs.q: In the Miller–Urey experiment, a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour was exposed to electrical sparks for a week. Which conclusion is supported by the products that were found?
options: Living cells can form from inorganic molecules given an energy source and enough time.
The twenty amino acids used in proteins are the only products that such conditions make.
Amino acids and other carbon compounds can form abiotically under such conditions.
Carbon compounds can form only where living organisms are already present.
mcqs.specStatementText: Miller and Urey showed carbon compounds can form abiotically
mcqs.explain: The water in the apparatus came to contain amino acids and other carbon compounds, showing that compounds needed by life can form from inorganic molecules by chemical processes, with lightning-like discharges as the energy source, under conditions that may have existed on pre-biotic Earth.
rationales: A student who has heard that the experiment 'created life' picks this. No cells, polymers or self-replicating molecules were formed; the products were small carbon compounds such as amino acids.

A student who thinks 'amino acids' means only the twenty protein building blocks picks this. The products were an undirected mixture that included some protein amino acids, amino acids not used in proteins, and other carbon compounds.

The water in the apparatus came to contain amino acids and other carbon compounds, showing that compounds needed by life can form from inorganic molecules by chemical processes, with lightning-like discharges as the energy source, under conditions that may have existed on pre-biotic Earth.

A student who holds that organic compounds need a living source picks this, but the apparatus was sterile and contained no organisms. The result shows the opposite: carbon compounds form by chemistry alone.

mcqs.q: Geologists now think that the early atmosphere contained more carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and less methane and ammonia, than the mixture Miller and Urey used. What is the best evaluation of the experiment in the light of this?
options: The experiment has been disproved, so it provides no evidence about the origin of carbon compounds on early Earth.
The composition of the mixture does not matter, because the experiment proved how life began in any case.
The conditions on pre-biotic Earth cannot be known, so no laboratory experiment can tell us anything about them.
The mixture was a limitation, but the finding that such compounds can form abiotically still stands.
mcqs.specStatementText: Miller and Urey showed carbon compounds can form abiotically
mcqs.explain: Evaluation weighs limitations against strengths. The gas mixture is a genuine limitation, but the experiment's central result – that amino acids and other carbon compounds form from inorganic molecules given an energy source – has been repeated with revised mixtures, so it remains evidence for the pre-biotic origin of carbon compounds.
rationales: A student who treats any flaw in a method as overturning the conclusion picks this. The revised atmosphere limits how well the original mixture modelled early Earth, but experiments with other plausible mixtures also yield amino acids, so the evidence still stands.

A student who believes the experiment produced life picks this. It produced carbon compounds only, and the realism of the conditions matters when judging how relevant those products are to early Earth.

A student who thinks an unrepeatable past event cannot be studied scientifically picks this. The exact conditions cannot be replicated, but hypotheses about them make testable predictions, and simulation experiments are one way of testing them.

Evaluation weighs limitations against strengths. The gas mixture is a genuine limitation, but the experiment's central result – that amino acids and other carbon compounds form from inorganic molecules given an energy source – has been repeated with revised mixtures, so it remains evidence for the pre-biotic origin of carbon compounds.

mcqs.q: Fatty acids added to water at a suitable pH coalesce into spherical bilayers, forming vesicles. What causes this to happen spontaneously?
options: The molecules are amphipathic: hydrophobic tails are excluded from the water while hydrophilic heads stay in contact with it.
The molecules are entirely hydrophobic, so they separate from the water and pack into a solid droplet of lipid.
Strong bonds form between neighbouring hydrocarbon tails, pulling the molecules together into a closed layer.
Enzymes present in the water link the fatty acids together into a membrane, in the same way as happens in cells.
mcqs.explain: A fatty acid has a hydrophilic carboxyl head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other and to the heads and exclude the tails, so the molecules arrange themselves into a bilayer with the tails inside, and the bilayer closes into a sphere. No enzymes or energy input from cells are needed.
rationales: A fatty acid has a hydrophilic carboxyl head and a hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other and to the heads and exclude the tails, so the molecules arrange themselves into a bilayer with the tails inside, and the bilayer closes into a sphere. No enzymes or energy input from cells are needed.
A student who pictures fatty acids as oil picks this. The carboxyl group is hydrophilic, so the molecules do not form a solid droplet: they form a bilayer enclosing water, with water on both sides.

A student who hears 'hydrophobic interactions' as an attraction between tails picks this. The forces between hydrocarbon chains are weak; the tails end up together because water excludes them, not because they bond strongly.
A student who thinks membranes can only be built by cells picks this. Vesicle formation is self-assembly: it needs no enzymes, which is why it could have occurred before any cell existed.

mcqs.q: Why was the formation of membrane-bound compartments a necessary step in the origin of cells?
options: It shielded the enclosed molecules from the ultraviolet light that reached the surface.
It allowed the chemistry inside the compartment to become different from that of the outside.
It provided a solid droplet of lipid inside which the first chemical reactions could occur.
It allowed a complete cell to assemble in a single step from the molecules dissolved in the water.
mcqs.explain: A membrane keeps self-replicating molecules and their products together at higher concentrations and separates them from the surroundings, so a distinct internal chemistry can develop – the reason the IB guide gives for why a membrane-bound compartment was needed.
rationales: A student who carries over the GCSE idea that a membrane 'protects the cell' picks this. A thin bilayer is no shield against ultraviolet radiation; the importance of the compartment lies in what it does to the chemistry inside.

A membrane keeps self-replicating molecules and their products together at higher concentrations and separates them from the surroundings, so a distinct internal chemistry can develop – the reason the IB guide gives for why a membrane-bound compartment was needed.

A student who imagines fatty acids forming an oil droplet picks this. A vesicle is a hollow sphere of bilayer enclosing water; the reactions occur in the aqueous interior, not in a solid mass of lipid.
A student who thinks the first cell appeared in a single event picks this. Compartmentalization is one of several requirements that combined gradually; enclosing molecules does not make a cell.

mcqs.q: Why is RNA, rather than DNA, presumed to have been the first genetic material?
options: RNA formed as single-stranded copies made from the very first DNA molecules to exist.
RNA is simpler than DNA, so it is more stable and survived for longer in the early oceans.
RNA can be replicated and is catalytic, so it could serve as both genes and enzymes.
RNA was needed to code for the proteins that acted as the very first enzymes.
mcqs.specStatementText: RNA was probably the first genetic material
mcqs.explain: RNA can be copied by complementary base pairing and some RNA molecules, ribozymes, are catalytic. One type of molecule could therefore have acted as both the genetic material and the enzymes of the earliest cells, avoiding the problem of which came first, genes or enzymes.
rationales: A student who assumes DNA is the original genetic molecule and RNA its copy picks this. The hypothesis is the reverse: RNA carried information first and DNA took over storage later.
A student who equates simplicity with durability picks this. RNA is less stable than DNA; the case for RNA rests on its ability to be replicated and to catalyse reactions, not on stability.

RNA can be copied by complementary base pairing and some RNA molecules, ribozymes, are catalytic. One type of molecule could therefore have acted as both the genetic material and the enzymes of the earliest cells, avoiding the problem of which came first, genes or enzymes.

A student who believes all enzymes are proteins picks this. The point of the RNA hypothesis is that RNA itself catalysed the first reactions; protein enzymes evolved later, and ribozymes still catalyse peptide bond formation in ribosomes.

mcqs.q: In ribosomes, the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids is catalysed by ribosomal RNA. Why is this significant for hypotheses about the origin of cells?
options: It shows that RNA is more stable than DNA, which is why it survived from the earliest cells.
It shows that rRNA must be a protein, since only proteins can act as catalysts.
It shows that DNA came first, because the rRNA is transcribed from genes in DNA.
It shows that RNA can catalyse reactions, as presumed for the earliest cells.
mcqs.specStatementText: RNA was probably the first genetic material
mcqs.explain: The ribosome's peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme still used by every cell today. Its survival is evidence that RNA can catalyse reactions, supporting the presumption that RNA served as both genetic material and enzymes before proteins took over most catalysis.
rationales: A student who thinks RNA came first because it is more durable picks this. RNA is less stable than DNA; the ribosome's ribozyme is significant because it shows RNA can catalyse reactions, not because RNA is long-lasting.
A student who holds that all enzymes are proteins picks this. Ribosomal RNA is a nucleic acid; its catalytic activity is precisely what shows that enzymes need not be proteins.

A student who reads the order DNA to RNA to protein as an evolutionary order picks this. That rRNA is transcribed from DNA in modern cells says nothing about which molecule came first; the catalytic ability of RNA points to RNA.

The ribosome's peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme still used by every cell today. Its survival is evidence that RNA can catalyse reactions, supporting the presumption that RNA served as both genetic material and enzymes before proteins took over most catalysis.

mcqs.q: Which evidence supports the existence of a last universal common ancestor (LUCA)?
options: The same genetic code and some shared genes are found in all organisms.
All organisms carry identical DNA sequences in each of their genes.
Fossils of LUCA itself have been identified in the oldest rocks on Earth.
DNA extracted from the oldest known fossils matches the genomes of modern organisms.
mcqs.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
mcqs.explain: The IB guide names the universal genetic code and shared genes across all organisms as the evidence for LUCA. Both are features that are best explained by inheritance from a single common ancestor.
rationales: The IB guide names the universal genetic code and shared genes across all organisms as the evidence for LUCA. Both are features that are best explained by inheritance from a single common ancestor.
A student who takes 'universal genetic code' to mean identical DNA picks this. Genes differ widely between organisms; it is the code translating codons into amino acids that is universal.
A student who thinks of LUCA as a specific first organism that could be found picks this. No fossil has been identified as LUCA; the evidence comes from comparing organisms alive today.
A student who believes DNA can be recovered from any fossil picks this. DNA does not survive for billions of years; genomic evidence comes from the genomes of living organisms.

mcqs.q: Codon UGG specifies tryptophan in bacteria, fungi, plants and animals alike. Why is this kind of observation taken as evidence for a common ancestor of all life?
options: The code is the only one that is chemically possible, so every organism that evolved had to use it.
Codon assignments are largely arbitrary, so a shared code is best explained by a single ancestor.
It shows that all organisms have the same genes, inherited without change from LUCA.
It shows that LUCA was the first cell, because the code must have existed from the start.
mcqs.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
mcqs.explain: Which codon specifies which amino acid is set by tRNAs and their loading enzymes, not by chemical necessity, and other assignments would work. That all organisms use the same convention is therefore best explained by their descent from a single ancestor, LUCA.
rationales: A student who assumes chemistry fixes the codon assignments picks this. If the code were chemically inevitable, sharing it would not indicate common descent; the minor variant codes in mitochondria show that other assignments are possible.

Which codon specifies which amino acid is set by tRNAs and their loading enzymes, not by chemical necessity, and other assignments would work. That all organisms use the same convention is therefore best explained by their descent from a single ancestor, LUCA.
A student who confuses the code with the genome picks this. A shared codon assignment says nothing about which genes an organism has; genes differ greatly between organisms.

A student who equates LUCA with the first cell picks this. The shared code shows that all living organisms descend from LUCA; it does not show that no other forms of life existed before or alongside it.

mcqs.q: It is considered likely that other forms of life evolved on early Earth in addition to the lineage leading to LUCA. Why do none of them have living descendants today?
options: They were wiped out by an asteroid impact before LUCA had appeared on Earth.
It cannot be known, because unobserved events on early Earth lie outside science.
They became extinct through competition from LUCA and its descendants.
They did not exist, because LUCA was the very first living cell to exist on Earth.
mcqs.specStatementText: All living things share one last common ancestor
mcqs.explain: LUCA and its descendants outcompeted other early forms of life for resources, so those lineages became extinct. This is why every organism alive today traces back to LUCA even though it was not the only or the first form of life.
rationales: A student who associates extinction only with catastrophes picks this. No catastrophe is required: the guide attributes their extinction to competition from LUCA and its descendants.

A student who thinks an event that nobody observed cannot be studied scientifically picks this. Claims about the past are testable indirectly: the universal code and shared genes show that all living organisms descend from LUCA, and the extinction of other early lineages is inferred, attributed to competition from LUCA and its descendants.

LUCA and its descendants outcompeted other early forms of life for resources, so those lineages became extinct. This is why every organism alive today traces back to LUCA even though it was not the only or the first form of life.

A student who takes LUCA to be the first cell picks this. LUCA is the last common ancestor of living organisms, not the first organism; the guide includes the likelihood that other forms of life evolved and became extinct.

mcqs.q: Stromatolites and microfossils in rocks from Western Australia are among the oldest evidence of cells. Which approach is used to estimate their age?
options: Carbon-14 dating of the carbon left in the fossilized cells themselves
Sequencing the DNA preserved in the fossils and applying a molecular clock
Identifying the fossils as LUCA and reading its age from the family tree
Radiometric dating of the rock using isotopes with very long half-lives
mcqs.specStatementText: How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
mcqs.explain: The rock containing the fossils is dated from the decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, giving an age of about 3.5 billion years and so a minimum age for life on Earth.
rationales: A student who knows carbon dating as 'the' dating method picks this. Carbon-14 decays away within about 50 000 years, so it is useless for rocks billions of years old.
A student who believes DNA survives in ancient fossils picks this. No DNA remains after billions of years; molecular clocks use the genomes of living organisms, not fossil DNA.
A student who thinks LUCA is a specific fossil organism picks this. No fossil has been identified as LUCA, and a family tree does not supply dates; the age comes from dating the rock.
The rock containing the fossils is dated from the decay of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, giving an age of about 3.5 billion years and so a minimum age for life on Earth.

mcqs.q: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. The oldest widely accepted fossil cells are about 3.5 billion years old, and molecular clock estimates place LUCA at roughly 4 billion years ago. Which interpretation is valid?
options: The dates are compatible: fossils give a minimum age for life, while molecular clock dates carry wide uncertainty.
The molecular clock date must be wrong, because the fossil gives the exact date at which life began on Earth.
The fossil date is unreliable, because carbon-14 dating cannot be used to measure ages of 3.5 billion years.
Both dates show that life is a recent arrival, occupying only a small fraction of Earth's history.
mcqs.specStatementText: How the dates of first cells and LUCA are estimated
mcqs.explain: A fossil shows that cells existed at least 3.5 billion years ago, so life could well be older. A molecular clock date is an estimate with an error range of hundreds of millions of years. Together they indicate that cells arose within the first billion years of Earth's history and that life has been evolving for over three billion years.
rationales: A fossil shows that cells existed at least 3.5 billion years ago, so life could well be older. A molecular clock date is an estimate with an error range of hundreds of millions of years. Together they indicate that cells arose within the first billion years of Earth's history and that life has been evolving for over three billion years.
A student who treats fossil dates as exact and complete picks this. A fossil gives a minimum age, not the date life began, and neither approach yields an exact figure for events this ancient.
A student who assumes fossils are dated by carbon-14 picks this. The rocks are dated radiometrically using long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238, which are suited to ages of billions of years.
A student whose sense of the past begins with the familiar fossils picks this. 3.5 billion out of 4.5 billion years is around 80% of Earth's history; life appeared within the first billion years.

mcqs.q: Which pair of findings provides evidence that LUCA evolved in the vicinity of hydrothermal vents?
options: Photosynthetic microfossils in rocks formed in shallow sunlit water, and light-harvesting genes shared by all organisms
Microfossils in ancient seafloor vent precipitates, and conserved genes across all life that fit vent conditions
DNA sequenced from vent microfossils, and its close match to the genomes of bacteria living at vents today
A fossil of LUCA itself recovered from a vent chimney, together with the age of the surrounding rock
mcqs.specStatementText: Evidence that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents
mcqs.explain: Iron-oxide tubes and filaments in rocks formed from seafloor hydrothermal vent precipitates, at least 3.77 billion years old, resemble vent bacteria, and genomic analysis shows that genes conserved across bacteria and archaea encode a metabolism suited to hot, anaerobic, hydrogen-rich vent conditions.
rationales: A student who assumes the first life was photosynthetic and lived in sunlight picks this. Genes for photosynthesis are not shared by all organisms, and the evidence for LUCA points to a dark, vent environment.

Iron-oxide tubes and filaments in rocks formed from seafloor hydrothermal vent precipitates, at least 3.77 billion years old, resemble vent bacteria, and genomic analysis shows that genes conserved across bacteria and archaea encode a metabolism suited to hot, anaerobic, hydrogen-rich vent conditions.
A student who believes DNA can be recovered from any fossil picks this. DNA does not survive for billions of years; the genomic evidence comes from comparing the genomes of living organisms.

A student who thinks LUCA is a particular organism that could be found picks this. No fossil has been identified as LUCA; the vent microfossils are evidence of early life in that environment, not of LUCA specifically.

mcqs.q: Genomic analysis identified genes that are conserved across both bacteria and archaea. Their protein products enable life without oxygen, at high temperature, and using hydrogen and carbon dioxide as sources of energy and carbon. What does this suggest about LUCA?
options: LUCA lived in sunlit surface water and obtained its energy by photosynthesis.
LUCA lived in an atmosphere already rich in oxygen, since these genes are still in use today.
LUCA lived in a hot, anaerobic environment such as a hydrothermal vent on the seafloor.
LUCA's genome was read directly from DNA that was preserved in the ancient vent fossils.
mcqs.specStatementText: Evidence that LUCA lived near hydrothermal vents
mcqs.explain: Genes conserved in both bacteria and archaea were probably present in their common ancestor, so their functions reveal LUCA's way of life: anaerobic, thermophilic and using hydrogen and carbon dioxide, all of which match conditions at hydrothermal vents.
rationales: A student who assumes life must start with photosynthesis picks this. The conserved genes point to chemical energy from hydrogen and carbon dioxide in the absence of light; photosynthesis evolved later in one lineage.
A student who assumes oxygen was always present picks this. The genes encode metabolism for life without oxygen, and free oxygen did not accumulate until photosynthetic organisms had evolved.

Genes conserved in both bacteria and archaea were probably present in their common ancestor, so their functions reveal LUCA's way of life: anaerobic, thermophilic and using hydrogen and carbon dioxide, all of which match conditions at hydrothermal vents.

A student who thinks ancient DNA can be sequenced from any fossil picks this. The analysis compared the genomes of living organisms; DNA does not survive billions of years, and no fossil of LUCA is known.
